title: Conjugate priors
objectives: Update Beta-binomial, Gamma-Poisson and normal models in closed form.

screens.title: A new venue
screens.prose: A desk starts routing limit orders to a new venue. Before any data it believes fill rates sit near 20%. Its Beta(2, 8) prior is worth 10 imagined orders with 2 fills. Then 40 real orders arrive. Drag the number of fills and watch the posterior move.

derive.caption: Posterior Beta({{round(0.2*m + k, 1)}}, {{round(0.8*m + 40 - k, 1)}}): mean {{fixed((0.2*m + k)/(m + 40), 4)}}, weight on the data {{fixed(40/(m + 40), 2)}}

screens.question: Set 13 fills with the prior worth 10 orders. What is the posterior mean fill rate?

hints.text: The caption shows the mean as you drag.
Thirteen fills turn Beta(2, 8) into Beta(15, 35).

feedback.correct: 0.30: between the prior's 0.20 and the data's 0.325.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the fills to 13 and read the posterior mean.

byKey.mle: That is the MLE, 13/40, the data alone. The prior still pulls it down.
byKey.prior: That is the prior mean. The 40 orders move it up.

explain.text: Beta(2, 8) plus 13 fills and 27 misses is Beta(15, 35), mean 0.30. It sits between the prior mean 0.20 and the MLE 0.325.

screens.title: Updating is adding counts
screens.prose: In `estimation` lesson 12 a Beta prior was imagined heads and tails, updated to $\mathrm{Beta}(a + k, b + n - k)$. The posterior stayed in the prior's family. A prior with that property is **conjugate**: updating is adding counts. Here the mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and the MLE.
screens.question: $0.30 = w \times 0.325 + (1 - w) \times 0.20$. What weight $w$ sits on the data?

hints.text: Real orders against all orders, real and imagined.
The data carry 40 orders, the prior 10.

feedback.correct: 0.8: the 40 real orders out of 50 in all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the 40 real orders with the 10 imagined ones.

byKey.prior: That is the weight on the prior, $10/50$.
byKey.ratio: That is 10/40, prior over data. The weight is a share of the total.

explain.text: The posterior mean is $(a + k)/(a + b + n) = \frac{n}{a + b + n}\cdot\frac{k}{n} + \frac{a + b}{a + b + n}\cdot\frac{a}{a + b}$. With $n = 40$ and $a + b = 10$ the weight on the data is 0.8.

screens.title: Reading the posterior
screens.prose: Beta(15, 35) has sd 0.0642 and mode $14/48 = 0.2917$. Its 95% equal-tailed interval runs from 0.1825 to 0.4326. The venue pays off above a 25% fill rate. Drag the shaded region to run from 0.25 to 1.
screens.question: What is $P(p > 0.25 \mid \text{data})$?

hints.text: The label on the shaded region is its probability.
Move the left handle to 0.25 and the right one to 1.
About 0.775.

feedback.correct: 0.7747: about a 77% chance the venue clears 25%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade from 0.25 to 1 and read the label.

byKey.cdf: That is the chance below 0.25. The question asks above it.
byKey.prior: That is the prior's chance above 0.25. The data have moved it up.

explain.text: `beta(15, 35).sf(0.25)` is 0.7747; two million draws give 0.7753. The prior alone gave 0.3003.

screens.title: Defaults with a Gamma prior
screens.prose: A loan book's yearly defaults are Poisson with rate $\lambda$. The prior is Gamma(2, rate 1), mean 2. Five years bring $3, 1, 4, 2, 5$ defaults. Step through the years: each adds its count to the shape and 1 to the rate.

derive.caption: After {{yrs}} years: Gamma({{2 + cum[yrs]}}, rate {{1 + yrs}}), mean {{fixed((2 + cum[yrs])/(1 + yrs), 4)}}

screens.question: After five years the mean is $2.8333 = w \times 3 + (1 - w) \times 2$, with 3 the MLE. What is $w$?

widget.accept: 0.8333: $5/(5 + 1)$, years of data over years of data plus the prior's rate.
widget.label: Weight w

hints.text: The rate counts years: 5 of data, 1 imagined in the prior.
$w = n/(\beta + n)$.

feedback.correct: 0.8333: the five real years against one imagined year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the 5 years of data with the prior's rate of 1.

byKey.prior: That is the weight on the prior mean, $1/6$.
byKey.beta: That is the fill-rate weight from the Beta screen. Here the prior is worth one year.

explain.text: Gamma(2, 1) becomes Gamma(17, rate 6): mean 2.8333, sd $\sqrt{17}/6 = 0.6872$, 95% interval (1.6505, 4.3305). The weight on the data's MLE of 3 is $5/6$.

screens.title: Three conjugate pairs
screens.prose:
Each update adds what the data carry to what the prior carries.
$$\mathrm{Beta}(a, b) \to \mathrm{Beta}(a + k,\ b + n - k)$$
$$\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta) \to \mathrm{Gamma}\big(\alpha + \textstyle\sum y_t,\ \beta + n\big)$$
Normal prior $N(m_0, s_0^2)$, estimate $\hat x$ with error $s$:
$$\tfrac{1}{s_1^2} = \tfrac{1}{s_0^2} + \tfrac{1}{s^2}$$
$$m_1 = s_1^2\left(\tfrac{m_0}{s_0^2} + \tfrac{\hat x}{s^2}\right)$$
screens.question: In the normal case, what adds up?

options.text: The precisions, one over each variance

options.why: Adding variances would make the posterior wider than the prior. More information narrows it.
Standard deviations never add for independent pieces; precisions do here.

feedback.correct: Precisions add, and the mean is their weighted average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which quantity grows as information grows?

byKey.var: You added the variances. Information adds as precision, so the posterior narrows.

screens.title: Why the Gamma update works
screens.prose: Derive the Gamma-Poisson update for counts $y_1, \dots, y_n$ with a Gamma($\alpha$, rate $\beta$) prior. One line is a slip: leave it out.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Likelihood: $\prod_t e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y_t}/y_t! \propto \lambda^{\sum y_t}e^{-n\lambda}$, as the years are independent
Prior: $\pi(\lambda) \propto \lambda^{\alpha - 1}e^{-\beta\lambda}$, the Gamma density in rate form
Posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\times$ prior $= \lambda^{\alpha + \sum y_t - 1}e^{-(\beta + n)\lambda}$, by Bayes' rule
That kernel is Gamma$(\alpha + \sum y_t,\ \beta + n)$; the constant follows from the density integrating to 1
So the rate becomes $\beta + \sum y_t$, since the counts add to the rate
lines.why: The counts sit in the power of $\lambda$, so they add to the shape. The rate gains $n$, one for each year of exposure.

hints.text: Write the likelihood and the prior as powers of $\lambda$ times exponentials.
Multiply them: powers add, exponents add.
The counts go in the power, the years in the exponential.

feedback.correct: Likelihood times prior is again a Gamma kernel, so the posterior is Gamma.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two kernels and read off the shape and rate.

byKey.x: You added the counts to the rate. They sit in the power of $\lambda$, so they raise the shape.

explain.text: With $\alpha = 2$, $\beta = 1$, $\sum y_t = 15$ and $n = 5$ the posterior is Gamma(17, rate 6). Swapping the roles, counts to the rate and years to the shape, gives Gamma(7, rate 16), mean 0.44.

screens.title: A fund's alpha
screens.prose: A fund's alpha is estimated at 6% a year with standard error 4%. The analyst's prior is $N(0, 2^2)$: most alphas are near zero. Precisions add: $1/4 + 1/16 = 0.3125$, so the posterior sd is $\sqrt{3.2} = 1.7889$.
screens.question: What is the posterior mean alpha, in % a year?

hints.text: Weight each mean by its precision.
$(0 \times \tfrac14 + 6 \times \tfrac1{16}) / 0.3125$.

feedback.correct: 1.2%: the 6% estimate shrunk by the factor 0.8 towards 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the prior mean and the estimate by their precisions.

byKey.est: That is the estimate alone. The prior is tighter than the estimate here.
byKey.avg: That is a plain average. The prior's precision is four times the estimate's.
byKey.swap: You put weight 0.8 on the estimate. The 0.8 is the shrinkage towards the prior.

explain.text: The posterior is $N(1.2, 1.7889^2)$. The shrinkage factor is $B = 16/(16 + 4) = 0.8$, so $1.2 = (1 - 0.8) \times 6$. Its 95% interval is $(-2.306, 4.706)$ and $P(\alpha > 0) = 0.7488$.

screens.title: Scale or rate
screens.prose: A colleague checks the default posterior Gamma(17, rate 6) in scipy. Their curve has mean 102 defaults a year. `scipy.stats.gamma` takes a shape `a`, then `loc`, then `scale`.
screens.question: Which call gives the posterior?

options.why: You passed the rate as the scale. Its mean is $17 \times 6 = 102$.
The second positional argument is `loc`. It shifts the curve right by 6: mean 23.
That is the prior. The counts have not been added.

hints.text: scipy wants a scale, which is one over the rate.
Rate 6 means scale $1/6$.
`gamma(17, scale=1/6)` has mean $17/6$.

feedback.correct: Scale is one over rate, as in `limits-thm` lesson 18.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Convert the rate to a scale.

byKey.scale: You passed 6 as the scale, so the mean became 102. scipy's scale is one over the rate.
byKey.loc: You passed 6 as `loc`, which shifts the curve by 6.

explain.text: scipy parametrises the Gamma by scale, $1/\text{rate}$. `gamma(17, scale=1/6).mean()` is 2.8333; `scale=6` gives 102. Plot the curve before trusting a parameter.

screens.title: A flat prior and no fills
screens.prose: A second venue gets a flat prior, Beta(1, 1), and 0 fills in 40 orders. The MLE is 0. The posterior is Beta(1, 41), and its mean is $(k + 1)/(n + 2)$.
screens.question: What is the posterior mean fill rate?

hints.text: Put $k = 0$ and $n = 40$ into $(k + 1)/(n + 2)$.

feedback.correct: 0.0238: a flat prior is not the MLE, and the posterior keeps mass above 0.

byKey.mle: That is the MLE. Even a flat prior adds one imagined fill.
byKey.n: That is $1/40$. The flat prior adds two imagined orders, so divide by 42.

explain.text: Beta(1, 1) is one imagined fill and one miss, so the mean is $1/42 = 0.0238$. The shaded chance of a rate above 5% is still 0.12.

screens.title: The three updates in code
screens.prose: Write the three updates and an equal-tailed interval. Return plain tuples. Remember that scipy's Gamma takes `scale = 1/rate`.
screens.question: Complete the four functions.

widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests. The Beta and Gamma updates must be exact tuples, the normal one within 1e-9. Three intervals are rounded to 6 places. SciPy loads on the first run.

hints.text: Each update is one line of addition.
For the normal case add precisions, then take the precision-weighted mean.
The interval cuts $(1 - \text{level})/2$ from each tail with `dist.ppf`.

feedback.correct: All three updates add counts or precisions; the interval comes from `ppf`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your output with the console.

explain.text: The Beta interval is $(0.182519, 0.432630)$ and the Gamma one $(1.650521, 4.330500)$. Both come from `ppf` at 0.025 and 0.975.

screens.title: Updating every day
screens.prose: The venue desk updates daily. Monday ended at Beta(15, 35), which becomes Tuesday's prior. Tuesday brings 6 fills in 30 orders.
screens.question: What is the posterior mean fill rate after Tuesday?

hints.text: Add Tuesday's counts to Monday's posterior.

feedback.correct: 0.2625: the same as updating Beta(2, 8) on all 70 orders at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Monday's posterior already holds the prior and Monday's data.

byKey.twice: You added the desk's Beta(2, 8) again. It is already inside Monday's posterior, so it was counted twice.
byKey.mon: That is Monday's mean. Tuesday's 6 fills in 30 pull it down.

explain.text: Beta(15, 35) plus 6 fills and 24 misses is Beta(21, 59), mean 0.2625. Updating Beta(2, 8) once on 19 fills in 70 orders gives the same posterior.

ideas: A conjugate prior keeps the posterior in its family. Beta(2, 8) and 13 fills in 40 give Beta(15, 35), mean 0.30.
Gamma(shape, rate) adds the counts to the shape and the periods to the rate; scipy wants `scale = 1/rate`.
Normal priors add precisions: a 6% alpha with a 4% error and a $N(0, 2^2)$ prior shrinks to 1.2%.

formula.name: Beta-binomial update
formula.tex: p \mid k \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + k,\ b + n - k),\quad E[p \mid k] = \tfrac{n}{a + b + n}\hat p + \tfrac{a + b}{a + b + n}\tfrac{a}{a + b}
formula.note: The weight on the data is real orders over all orders.

summary.trap: Passing a Gamma rate as scipy's scale: `gamma(17, scale=6)` has mean 102, not 2.83.

quiz.prose: The fill rate's 95% credible interval is (0.1825, 0.4326).
quiz.question: What does it say?

options.text: Given the prior and the 40 orders, $p$ lies in it with probability 0.95
95% of intervals built this way from repeated samples cover $p$
options.why: That is a confidence interval, from `testing`. A credible interval is a probability about $p$ given these data.

options.text: 95% of future fill rates will fall in it
options.why: Fill rates are not drawn again. The interval is about the one rate $p$.

feedback.correct: A credible interval is a posterior probability statement about $p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A credible interval conditions on the data seen.

byKey.freq: You read it as a confidence interval. That statement is about repeated samples, not about this $p$.

explain.text: The posterior puts probability 0.95 on (0.1825, 0.4326). A confidence interval's 95% is a property of the method over repeated samples.

quiz.prose: The posterior is Beta(15, 35). Its variance is $\frac{ab}{(a + b)^2(a + b + 1)}$.
quiz.question: What is its standard deviation?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $a = 15$, $b = 35$ into the formula, then take the root.

byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its square root.
byKey.bin: That is $\sqrt{0.3 \times 0.7/40}$, dividing by the 40 real orders. The posterior divides by $a + b + 1 = 51$.

quiz.prose: A new loan book has a Gamma(2, rate 1) prior on its yearly default rate. Three years pass with no defaults.
quiz.question: What is the posterior mean default rate?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add 0 to the shape and 3 to the rate.

byKey.mle: That is the MLE. The prior keeps the rate above 0.
byKey.prior: That is the prior mean. Three quiet years pull it down.

explain.text: Gamma(2, 1) with no counts over 3 years is Gamma(2, rate 4), mean 0.5.

quiz.prose: Another fund's alpha is estimated at 6% with standard error 3%. The prior is $N(0, 3^2)$.
quiz.question: What is the posterior mean alpha, in %?

widget.accept: 3: equal precisions, so the factor is 0.5.
widget.label: Posterior mean

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With equal variances the shrinkage factor is 1/2.

byKey.b8: That used the lesson's factor 0.8. Here $B = 9/(9 + 9) = 0.5$.
